newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ yield curve steepens at close as bills rally.
newsitem.headline: NZ yield curve steepens at close as bills rally.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (JUN) 92.11 (PREV 92.00) 90-DAYS 7.72 (PREV 7.80) 3-YR BONDS (JUN) 91.83 (PREV 91.84) 02/00 8.12 (PREV 8.09)
OVERNIGHT CASH 7.50 PCT (PREV 7.50) US 5-YR 6.75 (PREV 6.71)
* NZ bills, bonds, part company at Wednesday's close
* Bills rally on currency strength following Birch interview
* Bond mkt tone still bearish, selling seen in long end
The short and long ends of New Zealand's yield curve parted company by Wednesday's close, as the money market received a fillip from the currency and bonds encountered selling.

Bank bills rallied eight basis points to 7.72 percent and bill futures closed 11 points stronger at 92.11, after Finance Minister Bill Birch said export growth suggested the New Zealand dollar was not overvalued.
The comments, in an interview with Reuters Financial Television in Hong Kong, gave the Kiwi dollar an added shove just when stop-lossing was already underway, dealers said.
By 0500 GMT the Kiwi was at US0.6921/28, from 0.6878/85 at the open and around 0.6900 just before the interview. The Kiwi's Trade-Weighted Index finished at 68.83, from 68.39 at the open.
Foreign exchange dealers said the Kiwi felt well bid even on its high of around 0.6930, and there were still a few traders with short positions after the selling of recent weeks.
Money market dealers said the short end had not gone as far as traders would have liked given the currency's strength.
"I think it (the bill rally) would have gone further had the bonds participated as well," one said.
However, bonds not only failed to follow the bills, they went in the opposite direction.
Dealers said that, while the short end was able to go with the currency trend, bonds remained in the grip of bearish sentiment and were more influenced by weak U.S. Treasuries.

"On the other hand, if people own bonds and want to sell them, it's probably a good time to sell because the currency's high. It's not so good from a yield point of view maybe, but it's definitely good from a currency point of view," one said.
"It could suggest foreign investors are looking to sell bonds and were waiting for the right window in terms of the currency level," he added.
Dealers said the bond market was sensitive to small deals. One said morning trade on Thursday could see the bill market rallying further if the currency gains looked sustainable.
